title: Kimchi Bacteria May Help Your Body Get Rid of Tiny Plastic Bits
summary:
Have you ever eaten kimchi? It's a spicy, fermented cabbage dish from Korea. Now scientists have found that a bacterium (a tiny living thing) in kimchi might help your body get rid of harmful plastic bits.

These plastic bits are called nanoplastics. They are super tiny—less than one-thousandth of a millimeter. That's way smaller than a grain of sand. They come from larger plastic trash that breaks down. They can get into your body through food and water. Because they are so small, they can slip through your intestines and build up in organs like your kidneys and brain.

But here's the cool part: scientists at the World Institute of Kimchi in Korea found a special bacterium in kimchi called Leuconostoc mesenteroides CBA3656. In the lab, this bacterium stuck to nanoplastics with 87% efficiency. That means it grabbed onto most of them! Even in fake human intestinal conditions, it still stuck to 57% of the plastic bits. Another bacterium only stuck to 3%.

The scientists also tested it on mice. Mice that got the kimchi bacterium had more than twice as much nanoplastic in their poop. That means the plastic was leaving their bodies instead of staying inside.

"Plastic pollution is increasingly recognized not only as an environmental issue but also as a public health concern," said Dr. Sehee Lee, the lead researcher. "Our findings suggest that microorganisms derived from traditional fermented foods could represent a new biological approach to address this emerging challenge."

So next time you eat kimchi, you might be helping your body fight plastic pollution. Scientists will keep studying this to see if it can help humans too.
why_it_matters: Plastic bits end up in our food and water, so finding a friendly bacterium that helps push them out could matter for your family's health — and it shows that old foods like kimchi can teach science new tricks.

background_read: Kimchi is a traditional Korean food made by salting cabbage and letting it ferment, which means tiny bacteria slowly change its taste.
The World Institute of Kimchi (a research center in South Korea that studies kimchi) is where this study was done.
Plastic trash in the ocean and on land slowly breaks into smaller and smaller pieces, and the very tiniest pieces are called nanoplastics.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dr. Sehee Lee and other scientists at the World Institute of Kimchi in Korea.
WHAT: They found a kimchi bacterium that sticks to nanoplastics and helped mice pass more of the plastic out in their poop.
WHERE: In the lab, in fake human intestinal conditions, and in tests on mice.
WHY: Nanoplastics can build up in organs, so a bacterium from a fermented food might be a new natural way to help bodies get rid of them.

perspectives.description: They are excited that a traditional fermented food might have a hidden health benefit.
They point out the tests were done in the lab and in mice, not in people, so we still don't know if it works in humans.
They say the real fix is making less plastic trash in the first place, instead of relying on bacteria to clean it up later.
